newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Bossi is messiah to some, clown to others.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Bossi is messiah to some, clown to others.

text.p: Critics of Italy's separatist leader Umberto Bossi call him a political clown and opportunist who never passes up a chance to put his foot in his mouth.
Supporters virtually worship the blunt-talking Northern League leader as a messiah they hope will lead the industrious north to independence.
This Sunday the 54-year-old firebrand will declare the birth of a "federal republic of Padania" in the lagoon city of Venice, after three days of "liberation" festivities along the River Po.
The immediate result will most likely be more of a whimper than a bang as an amorphous "republic" no country is set to recognise is born, if only in the eyes of its supporters.
But it will be the high point in the career of a man who has succeeded in turning the Italian political scene upside down despite -- or because of -- his brashness.
On the eve of a three-day "march to independence" along the river, which Bossi wants northerners to consider as holy as the Ganges is to Indians, he unleashed another surprise.
He "expelled" Irene Pivetti, a League member who held the pretigious post of lower house parliamentary speaker until May.
Bossi accused the Catholic Pivetti, whom he once threatened to "send to the Vatican in a coffin", of betraying the ideals of the League by favouring federalism over secession.
Bossi's opponents have ridiculed him for wanting to split Italy "Czechoslovakia-style" when Europe is seeking cohesion.
Analysts say his desire to introduce yet another currency into Europe's monetary system is economic madness.
He has insulted everyone from President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to southern-born schoolteachers earning near subsistence wages.
Gianfranco Fini, the hard-right National Alliance party, branded Bossi "disgusting" and compared him to a "drug addict who has to boost his dose of insults and provocations daily".
But Bossi, a cartoonists' favourite for his often dishevelled appearance, has put the northern malaise on the political agenda.
And that, say supporters, is enough to make him a hero among northerners fed up with decades of stifling bureaucracy and corruption by a succession of governments in Rome.
Because of Bossi, even leaders who firmly oppose separatism now openly acknowledge that Italy needs federalism.
Bossi identifies with Scotsman William Wallace's 13th century rebellion against the English.
"I am Braveheart but I am not going to meet his end. The great people of the North shall win," he said recently.
His talk can be outrageous. Even party faithful were embarrassed by a wild claim in 1994 that he had thwarted an armed revolt against Rome's leaders in the 1980s.
No-one in the north seemed to have noticed 300,000 people stashing weapons and plotting revolution in an area of Italy that has one of the world's highest living standards.
Bossi's movement, founded in 1984, remained obscure until the 1990 local elections when it began gathering strength in the north. "Autonomist" leagues sprung up in other northern regions.
In 1990, they merged to form the Northern League and in last April's national elections won a stunning 10.6 percent.
Bossi's strident anti-southern populism -- an anti-tax message laced with gut regionalism and attacks on immigration -- lured many who once voted for mainstream parties.
"The parties are rotten...the system is not reformable. You need to knock it over and pull out its roots," Bossi said in his 1992 autobiography, "Wind of the North."
"People are tired of sugar-coated men. They want leaders. It's better if you're a little bit of a bastard," Bossi said.
The son of a textile worker, Bossi dabbled in leftist politics before he became interested in regional autonomy while studying medicine at Pavia University.

He was born on September 19, 1941, near the northern town of Varese, and is married with two children. Although he has often attacked southerners as being the bloodsuckers of the hard-working north, his wife comes from Sicily.
